items.d: Information within **30 days** (48 hours if life or liberty is involved); **Section 4** proactive disclosure; **Section 8** exemptions with a **public-interest override**; **Section 24** exempts intelligence and security organisations except for corruption and human-rights allegations. The **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** let the Centre fix the **tenure, salary and service conditions of Information Commissioners** — the central criticism. The **DPDP Act, 2023** amended Section 8(1)(j) to exempt all personal information, further narrowing the Act.

A **chairperson plus up to 8 members, half judicial and half from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women**; jurisdiction covers the **PM with exclusions** (international relations, security, public order, atomic energy, space) and requires a **two-thirds bench approval**; power of **attachment and confiscation** of assets; mandates **states to set up Lokayuktas within a year**. Criticism: delayed appointment (first Lokpal only in 2019), weak prosecution wing, and the dilution of the whistle-blower link.

Passed but **never brought into force** — no rules notified, and the **2015 amendment bill** would bar disclosures touching ten exempt categories including sovereignty and commercial confidence. The gap is the standing example of 'legislation without implementation'.

The **2018 amendment** made **bribe-giving an offence**, covered **commercial organisations**, required **prior approval under Section 17A** before any enquiry into a public servant's official decisions, and extended the **Section 19** sanction requirement to retired officials. Criticised for protecting decision-makers; defended as the fix for 'decision paralysis'.

Made the CVC statutory (it existed from 1964 on the **Santhanam Committee's** recommendation). Multi-member body appointed by the President on the advice of the **PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition**; **supervises the CBI's investigation** of PC Act offences; the CVO in each ministry reports to it.

**Digital Personal Data Protection Act** — consent-based processing with **legitimate uses** exemptions, **Data Fiduciary** duties, **Consent Managers**, rights to access, correction, erasure and grievance redress, penalties up to **₹250 crore**, and a **Data Protection Board of India**. Criticised for **broad state exemptions under Section 17** and the dilution of RTI Section 8(1)(j). Rules notified in 2025.

Institutionalises **pre-litigation mediation** (voluntary after the 2023 revision), the **Mediation Council of India**, a **180-day** timeline, and enforceability of the settlement agreement as a court decree. Complements **Section 89 CPC**, the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (Lok Adalats) and the **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008**.

**Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (replacing IPC), **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** (CrPC) and **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam** (Evidence Act), in force from **1 July 2024**. Key changes: **community service** as a punishment, **Zero FIR and e-FIR**, **timelines for charge-sheet, judgment (45 days) and framing of charges**, **forensic visits mandatory for offences carrying 7+ years**, sedition replaced by **Section 152**, and organised crime and terrorism defined in the general penal code for the first time.

Legal entitlement to subsidised grain for **75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population** — about **80 crore people**; **5 kg per person per month** for priority households and **35 kg per household** for Antyodaya; **maternity benefit of ₹6,000**; grain provided **free under PMGKAY** since 2023, extended to 2028. Also mandates **grievance redress officers and vigilance committees**. Coverage still rests on **Census 2011** population — the standing exclusion critique.

**100 days of guaranteed wage employment** per rural household, work within **5 km**, wages within **15 days** else compensation, **unemployment allowance** if work is not provided in 15 days, **one-third participation by women** (actual participation is over 50%), and **social audit by the gram sabha** as a statutory requirement. Demand-driven and rights-based — the world's largest such programme. Being restructured as the **VB-G RAM G Act, 2025**.

Free and compulsory education for **6-14**; **25% reservation in private unaided schools** for disadvantaged groups with state reimbursement; **no detention till Class 8** (relaxed by the **2019 amendment**, which allows detention in Classes 5 and 8 after a re-examination); prohibits **screening, capitation fees, physical punishment and teacher deployment for non-educational work** other than census, elections and disaster relief; **PTR and infrastructure norms** in the Schedule.

Recognises **individual forest rights**, **community forest rights** and, crucially, **Community Forest Resource rights (Section 3(1)(i))** with the gram sabha as the authority to protect and manage; also recognises rights of **Other Traditional Forest Dwellers** with a 75-year residence test. Basis of the **Niyamgiri** gram sabha veto. Low CFR recognition is the implementation gap.

Expanded disabilities from 7 to **21**, adopted the **social model** in line with the **UNCRPD**, provided **4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education**, **accessibility standards**, and the concept of **reasonable accommodation**; recognises **high-support needs** and creates State/Chief Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities. *Rajive Raturi* (2024) enforced its accessibility rules.

**Decriminalised attempted suicide** (presumption of severe stress), gave every person a **right to access mental healthcare**, introduced **advance directives** and a **nominated representative**, and set up **Mental Health Review Boards**. Aligned with the UNCRPD. India's treatment gap for mental illness remains around 70-90%.

items.t: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
items.d: Obliges children and heirs to maintain parents and senior citizens; **maintenance tribunals** decide within 90 days; a **transfer of property can be voided** if the transferee neglects the elder; also provides for old-age homes in every district. The 2019 amendment bill sought to remove the maintenance ceiling and widen 'children' to include stepchildren and in-laws.

Statutory recognition of vending as a livelihood under **Art. 19(1)(g)**; **Town Vending Committees with 40% vendor representation**, a survey of all vendors, vending certificates, and a **prohibition on eviction without survey and rehabilitation**. Complemented by **PM SVANidhi** micro-credit.

Right to **self-perceived gender identity** with a certificate from the District Magistrate, prohibition of discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, and a **National Council for Transgender Persons**. Criticised for the certification requirement and for lighter punishment for offences against transgender persons than under general law.

**Selection Committee: the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM, and the Leader of the Opposition** — replacing the CJI whom *Anoop Baranwal* had included; a **Search Committee** headed by the Cabinet Secretary shortlists five names; **status and salary equal to a Supreme Court judge**; **removal of the CEC only like a Supreme Court judge**.

The CBI's only legal basis — it is **not a statutory body created by its own Act**. **Section 6** requires the **state's consent** for the CBI to investigate within its territory; several states have **withdrawn general consent**. Calcutta HC and the SC (*West Bengal v. Union of India*, 2024) have engaged the resulting federal question. **Section 4A** governs the Director's appointment; **Section 4B** the two-year minimum tenure.

Creates the **NHRC** — chaired by a **former CJI or a Supreme Court judge** (widened by the 2019 amendment), with the **chairpersons of NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCPCR, NCBC and the CIC and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities as deemed members**; **term 3 years or up to age 70**. Powers are **recommendatory**, it cannot inquire into a matter **more than one year old**, and it can only **seek a report from the armed forces**. That trio of limits is the standard critique.

Enacted under **Article 323A** — the **Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)** with 17 benches, and state tribunals on request. After *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997), an appeal lies to the **Division Bench of the High Court**, so the object of reducing the burden on High Courts was substantially defeated.

Abolished nine appellate tribunals (including FTAT, AAIFR and the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal), fixed a **four-year term and a minimum age of 50** for members, and re-enacted provisions the Supreme Court had struck down in *Madras Bar Association (2020)* — the sharpest recent instance of a legislative override of a judgment.

Regulates foreign contributions to associations. The **2020 amendment** barred **sub-granting to other FCRA entities**, cut permissible administrative expenses from 50% to **20%**, made **Aadhaar of office-bearers mandatory**, and required an **exclusive FCRA account at SBI, New Delhi Main Branch**. Upheld in *Noel Harper* (2022). Registrations of thousands of NGOs have lapsed or been cancelled since.

Applies where the scheduled offence involves **₹100 crore or more** and the person has left India to avoid prosecution; permits **confiscation of all assets, including benami and foreign property, without conviction**, and bars the fugitive from filing or defending civil claims. Used against Vijay Mallya, Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi.

Enacted under **Article 262**; the **2019 amendment bill** proposed a **single standing tribunal with multiple benches**, a **Disputes Resolution Committee** for negotiated settlement first, and strict timelines (one year, extendable by six months) — a response to tribunals such as Cauvery taking decades. The Act **bars the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court** under Art. 262(2), though SLPs still reach it.

items.t: Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023
items.d: Enacted after the Supreme Court's services judgment; creates the **National Capital Civil Services Authority** (CM plus the Chief Secretary and Principal Home Secretary, deciding by majority) with the **LG's discretion final** — effectively reversing the ruling. Pending before a Constitution Bench; the leading example of the legislature-versus-judiciary federalism conflict.

groups.g: International instruments India is party to

items.d: India is a party to the **ICCPR and ICESCR (both ratified 1979)**; the **UDHR (1948)** is declaratory and the source of Article 21 jurisprudence via *Maneka* and *Vishaka*. India has **not ratified** the Convention Against Torture (signed 1997), the Refugee Convention 1951, or ILO Conventions 87 and 98 on freedom of association.

India ratified **CEDAW in 1993 with declarations** on Articles 5(a) and 16(1) (non-interference in personal law) and on compulsory registration of marriage. *Vishaka* used CEDAW to fill the domestic vacuum, establishing that **international conventions consistent with fundamental rights can be read into them**.

**UNCRC ratified 1992** — basis of the JJ Act, POCSO and the child labour amendments; **UNCRPD ratified 2007** — basis of the RPwD Act, 2016 and its shift from the medical to the **social model of disability**.

**UN Convention Against Corruption**, ratified by India in **2011** — the trigger for the Lokpal Act, the amendment criminalising bribe-giving, and the Prevention of Money Laundering framework. Also the basis of mutual legal assistance in asset recovery.

India is **not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol** and has **no domestic refugee law** — refugees are governed by the Foreigners Act, 1946 (now the **Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025**), leaving status determination executive and ad hoc. Yet India has hosted Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Chakmas and Rohingya — the practice-versus-law gap is the answer's core point. *NHRC v. State of Arunachal Pradesh* (1996) held **Article 21 applies to non-citizens**.
